philosophers.intro: The twenty philosophers most engaged by the Curso Online de Filosofia, by measured presence in the 585-lecture corpus. Each page carries the thinker's own life and works, and the record of which lectures engage him.

philosophers.name: Aristóteles
philosophers.summary: Greek philosopher, disciple of Plato and tutor of Alexander of Macedon, founder of the Lyceum in Athens. His surviving treatises cover logic, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetics, and shaped much of ancient, medieval and modern philosophy.

readings.claim: The whole session insists on the order of the corpus: Aristotle begins as a teacher of rhetoric inside the Academy, and rhetoric already had centuries of tradition behind it from the sophists — whose real discovery, he says, was that two people arguing form a single piece of reasoning between them.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 04 — Aristotle

readings.claim: A reception history in one line: Aristotle only began to be understood in the twentieth century, with two or three exceptions. Aquinas's readings are brilliant, but he is not always talking about Aristotle — sometimes he is inventing another philosophy of his own.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 04 — Aristotle

readings.claim: On Werner Jaeger's intellectual biography — a brilliant book whose thesis is wrong. Jaeger has Aristotle moving from strict Platonism to modern empiricism; a century of argument concluded no such transition happened. But both poles really are in the corpus, so a reader has to live with the metaphysician and the empiricist at once rather than dissolving the problem.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 04 — Aristotle

readings.claim: He mentions an earlier course of his own in Rio, Pensamento e Atualidade de Aristóteles, of which some twelve lectures were nothing but the history of misreadings of Aristotle.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 04 — Aristotle

timeline.label: Born in Stagira, a small city of Chalcidice in northern Greece.
Moves to Athens and enters Plato's Academy, where he remains for about twenty years as disciple and colleague.
On Plato's death, leaves Athens and settles in Assos, in Asia Minor, with the ruler Hermias.
In Assos and then on the island of Lesbos, pursues research in marine biology; marries Pythias, Hermias's niece.
Summoned by Philip II to the Macedonian court at Pella, becomes tutor of the king's son, the future Alexander the Great (Britannica records 343 or 342 BC).
Returns to Athens and founds his own school, the Lyceum, by the gymnasium dedicated to Apollo Lyceus.

The Lyceum period: composition and organization of most of the surviving corpus — among others the Organon (logic), the Physics, the Metaphysics, the Nicomachean Ethics, the Politics and the Poetics; the internal dating of the treatises is uncertain and debated by specialists.
On Alexander's death and the anti-Macedonian reaction in Athens, withdraws from the city to Chalcis, on the island of Euboea.
Dies in Chalcis, Euboea.

philosophers.name: Descartes
philosophers.summary: French philosopher, mathematician and scientist, often described as the founder of modern philosophy. He created analytic geometry, formulated the first modern version of mind–body dualism, and proposed a method of systematic doubt as the foundation of knowledge.

timeline.label: Born in La Haye, in the Touraine region of France.
Studies at the Jesuit college of La Flèche, following the curriculum of grammar, humanities and scholastic philosophy.
Takes a degree in law at the University of Poitiers, which he will never practice.
Becomes a volunteer soldier at Breda, in the service of Prince Maurice of Nassau; decisive encounter with the scientist Isaac Beeckman.
In the region of Ulm, has the three dreams he interprets as a life mission devoted to the reform of knowledge.
Abandons the Rules for the Direction of the Mind (unfinished) and settles in the Netherlands, where he lives most of his adult life.
Publishes the Discourse on Method, together with the essays Dioptrics, Meteors and Geometry.
Publishes the Meditations on First Philosophy, with the Objections and Replies (2nd edition 1642).
Publishes the Principles of Philosophy, the synthesis of his metaphysics and natural philosophy.
Publishes The Passions of the Soul; accepts Queen Christina of Sweden's invitation and moves to Stockholm.
Dies in Stockholm, after falling ill in the Swedish winter.

philosophers.name: Platão
philosophers.summary: Athenian philosopher, disciple of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, founder of the Academy. His dialogues, which put into circulation themes such as the theory of Forms, the immortality of the soul and the just city, are among the founding texts of Western philosophy.

readings.claim: He says outright that he is not a great admirer of Plato, and calls the philosopher-king a monumental error: beyond knowing the universal law a ruler needs authority, and he asks how Plato failed to notice he had none — where Moses and Muhammad had it and were obeyed for millennia.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 02 — the Socratic project

readings.claim: He reads the Sicilian debacle as a caricature of Socrates' fate: Plato tries to steer a coup in a neighbouring state, it fails, the conspirators are killed or imprisoned and Plato is sold as a slave and bought back by a student. Socrates, on his reading, is the philosopher who knows he cannot be king.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 03 — Socrates and Plato

readings.claim: On the three worlds: the world of forms is not a superior world above the one man inhabits — it is that world. Man stands wholly in neither temporality nor the sensible, which is why the Plato-Aristotle dispute over whether the forms exist in themselves cannot be settled: on his reading neither the forms nor the sensible world exist in themselves, only within eternity.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 03 — Socrates and Plato

timeline.label: Born in Athens to an aristocratic family (the SEP gives '429?'; recent scholarship cited in the SEP's Socrates chronology proposes 424/423 BC).
Death of Socrates, to whose circle Plato belonged; after the execution he leaves Athens and spends a period in Megara, followed by travels the tradition attributes to him (Cyrene, Italy, Egypt).
First journey to Italy and Sicily; in Syracuse he attaches himself to Dion, brother-in-law of the tyrant Dionysius I.
Back in Athens, founds the Academy, the school Britannica places in the 380s BC and describes as a remote ancestor of the modern university.
Dialogues of the so-called early (Socratic) period, on the usual stylometric chronology: Apology, Crito, Euthyphro, Laches, Charmides, Gorgias, Protagoras, among others.
Dialogues of the middle period, including the Phaedo, the Symposium and the Republic (books II–X), in which the theory of Forms is articulated.
Second and third journeys to Syracuse, involving him with Dion in the attempt to influence the young tyrant Dionysius II — episodes narrated in the Seventh Letter, whose authenticity is disputed.
Late dialogues, among them the Theaetetus, Sophist, Statesman, Timaeus, Philebus and the Laws; the corpus transmitted under his name also includes letters and works of disputed authenticity.
Dies in Athens at about eighty; according to Diogenes Laertius he was buried at the Academy.

philosophers.name: Marx
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, economist and revolutionary, author (with Friedrich Engels) of the Communist Manifesto and of Capital. His theory of history, his critique of political economy and the political movement he inspired profoundly marked the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

timeline.label: Born in Trier, in the Rhine province of Prussia.
Enters the University of Bonn (October 1835) and transfers the following year to Berlin, where he studies law and philosophy.
Takes his doctorate in philosophy from the University of Jena.
Becomes editor of the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne.
Marries Jenny von Westphalen (June) and moves to Paris months later.
Expelled from France, settles in Brussels, followed by Engels; from this period date the manuscripts of The German Ideology (1845–46), published posthumously.
Publishes the Communist Manifesto with Engels, in the year of the European revolutions.
Expelled from Paris once more, settles in London, his home for the rest of his life.
Publishes A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, whose Preface carries the classic formulation of his materialist conception of history.

Foundation of the International Working Men's Association (First International); neither its founder nor its head, Marx becomes its leading intellectual figure, drafting the inaugural address and the provisional statutes.
Publishes volume I of Capital (volumes II and III would appear posthumously, in 1885 and 1894, edited by Engels).
Dies in London.

philosophers.name: Tomás de Aquino
philosophers.place: Roccasecca, near Aquino (Kingdom of Sicily, present-day Italy)
philosophers.summary: Dominican friar, theologian and philosopher, the leading figure of thirteenth-century scholasticism. His synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian doctrine, set out above all in the Summa theologiae and the Summa contra gentiles, became a central reference of the Catholic tradition.

readings.claim: Named with Hugh of St Victor as the point where allegorical interpretation reaches full mastery: his biblical commentaries are edifices to take one's hat off to, and there the science of symbolic interpretation finally earns the name of science — systematic, organised and rational.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08 — the advent of Christianity

timeline.label: Born at Roccasecca, a castle of a noble family near Aquino, between Rome and Naples (the SEP gives 'around 1225'; Britannica, '1224/25').
Studies as a child at the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, where his family expected him to make his career.

As an adolescent student at the University of Naples, decides to join the newly founded Order of Preachers (Dominicans) at about twenty; his family, opposed, keeps him detained at Roccasecca for about a year before relenting.
Studies philosophy in Paris as a Dominican friar; in 1248 he is sent to Cologne, under the direction of Albert the Great.
Nominated by Albert, returns to Paris for the advanced degree in theology; composes the commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences (Scriptum, 1252–56).
Master of theology, holds the Dominican chair at the University of Paris.
Back in Italy, teaches in Dominican houses; composes the Summa contra gentiles (c. 1258–64, per Britannica).
Begins the Summa theologiae, his greatest work, left unfinished at his death (1265/66–73, per Britannica).
Second Paris regency, marked by the controversies over radical Aristotelianism ('Averroism'); writes commentaries on Aristotle's principal works.
Returns to Italy, to Naples, where he spends his last teaching years.
Dies at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova, in Lazio.

philosophers.name: Kant
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, a central figure of modern philosophy, who spent his whole life in Königsberg. His 'critical philosophy', set out in the three Critiques, proposed that human reason legislates both for the knowledge of nature and for morality.

timeline.label: Born in Königsberg, capital of East Prussia.
Studies at the University of Königsberg (the Albertina); after university, works for some years as a private tutor in the region.
Takes the degree of Magister and becomes Privatdozent (private lecturer) at Königsberg, a position he holds for fifteen years under a heavy teaching load.
Appointed full professor of logic and metaphysics at Königsberg; presents the Inaugural Dissertation, the landmark of his critical turn.
Publishes the Critique of Pure Reason (revised 2nd edition 1787).
Publishes the Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics.
Publishes the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, his principal work on the fundamental principle of morality.
Publishes the Critique of Practical Reason.
Publishes the Critique of the Power of Judgment.
Publishes The Metaphysics of Morals (Doctrine of Right and Doctrine of Virtue), after Toward Perpetual Peace (1795).
Dies in Königsberg, the city he never left for long.

philosophers.name: Sócrates
philosophers.summary: Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, known through the testimonies of Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes. His practice of interrogating fellow citizens about the virtues, and his condemnation to death for impiety, made him a founding figure of Western philosophical ethics.

readings.claim: The session turns on a distinction between three figures the tradition confuses: the philosopher as martyr, the philosopher as leader and ruler, and the philosopher as his community's teacher and guide but not its chief. Socrates is the first and the third; the second is the error he lays at Plato's door.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 02 — the Socratic project

readings.claim: Philosophical authority is real but powerless, and he argues it has to be. A philosopher claiming power equal to his cognitive authority would have to be an absolute tyrant — and that is incompatible with how wisdom is acquired, which needs trial, error and an interior freedom a philosopher-king could not allow.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 03 — Socrates and Plato

timeline.label: Born in Athens, in the deme of Alopece (the SEP, following Nails, gives 469 BC; Britannica records c. 470 BC).
Serves as an infantry soldier (hoplite) in the Potidaea campaign, alongside Alcibiades.
Outbreak of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta, the backdrop of his adult life.
Fights at the battle of Delium, an Athenian defeat, under the command of Laches.
Caricatured in Aristophanes' comedy The Clouds, staged at the festival of Dionysus.
Fights at the battle of Amphipolis, another Athenian disaster — his last known campaign.
A member of the presiding committee (prytaneis) by lot, opposes the collective, summary trial of the generals of the battle of Arginusae before the Assembly.
Under the regime of the Thirty, refuses the order to go to Salamis and arrest the democratic general Leon — an episode later recalled in his defense.

Works: he wrote nothing; his thought is known above all through Plato's dialogues, Xenophon's Socratic writings and Aristophanes' satire — the disparity between the portraits constitutes the 'Socratic problem'.
Tried for impiety and for corrupting the young, he is condemned and executed by poison (hemlock) at seventy, in Athens.

philosophers.name: René Guénon
philosophers.summary: French metaphysician and writer, the principal formulator of the twentieth-century 'Traditionalist' or 'Perennialist' current. He wrote on Eastern metaphysics, symbolism, initiation and the critique of the modern world; he embraced Islam and lived his last twenty years in Cairo.

timeline.label: Born in Blois, France; raised in a strict Catholic milieu and educated by Jesuits.
After mathematics studies in Paris (Collège Rollin), abandons preparation for the academic examinations.
Frequents the Parisian occultist and neo-spiritualist milieux — the most obscure period of his biography.
Founds the occultist review La Gnose, which publishes his first writings, already conversant with Vedanta.
Marries a devout Catholic; a new phase of withdrawal from the occultist circles and association with Catholic intellectuals (among them Jacques Maritain).
Publishes his first book, Introduction générale à l'étude des doctrines hindoues, and the critique Le Théosophisme: histoire d'une pseudo-religion; L'Erreur spirite follows in 1923.
Publishes Orient et Occident.
Publishes L'Homme et son devenir selon le Vêdânta, his axial work on Vedanta; L'Ésotérisme de Dante is from the same year.
Publishes La Crise du monde moderne and Le Roi du monde; Catholic criticism of the latter deepens his estrangement from the Church.
Sudden death of his wife.
Travels to Cairo for a three-month stay and remains until his death; openly embraces Islam, is initiated into the Shadhiliyya Sufi order under the name Abdel Wahed Yahya, and remarries.
Publishes Le Règne de la Quantité et les Signes des Temps, considered his masterpiece of the critique of modernity.
Dies in Cairo, Egypt.

philosophers.name: Hegel
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, the leading exponent of post-Kantian German idealism. He elaborated a system spanning logic, philosophy of nature and philosophy of spirit, with lasting influence on philosophy, political theory and the historiography of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

readings.claim: Hegel's Lectures on the History of Philosophy are his prototype of the reflective model: philosophy's content IS its history, an internal dialectic in which spirit comes to consciousness of itself, with individual philosophers — his image — as ventriloquist's dummies in the hands of reason, links in a chain they need not be aware of.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 01 — history of the histories of philosophy

readings.claim: His counter-claim, and the thesis of his own course: the history of philosophy is not a linear continuity to be forced into unity, but a human drama, in which the unforeseen and the discontinuous enter as they do in anyone's life.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 01 — history of the histories of philosophy

timeline.label: Born in Stuttgart, in the duchy of Württemberg.
Studies at the Protestant seminary of Tübingen (the Stift), where he forms friendships with the poet Hölderlin and the philosopher Schelling.
Moves to Jena, joining Schelling, and publishes his first philosophical work (on the difference between Fichte's and Schelling's systems), along with the dissertation on the orbits of the planets.
Publishes the Phenomenology of Spirit, completed at Jena.
Publishes the Science of Logic, in parts (1812, 1813 and 1816).
Returns to university life as professor at Heidelberg.
Publishes the Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, the systematic exposition of his thought, later revised in new editions.
Takes the chair of philosophy at the University of Berlin, the most prestigious in the German philosophical world.
Publishes in Berlin the Elements of the Philosophy of Right, his major work of political philosophy.
Dies in Berlin, at the height of his fame.

philosophers.name: Louis Lavelle
philosophers.summary: French philosopher, one of the principal French metaphysicians of the twentieth century and a representative of the 'philosophie de l'esprit' current. Professor at the Sorbonne and the Collège de France, he developed an ontology of participation in being, articulated in the tetralogy La dialectique de l'éternel présent.

readings.claim: The finding the mention-count missed. Asked about method, he names the twentieth-century philosophy that counts: Lavelle first, then Husserl, then a trio. The transcription yields Zubiri and Lonergan and reduces the third to a single letter; this project's keyword notes propose Voegelin, which is a proposal and not a reading. The rest, he says, is decoration. This is the earliest located statement of the position the Curso Online de Filosofia would later rest on.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 04 — Aristotle

timeline.label: Born in Saint-Martin-de-Villeréal, in the Lot-et-Garonne, France.
Teaching career that passes through the University of Strasbourg, before the Sorbonne and the Collège de France.
Publishes La Dialectique du monde sensible.
Professor of philosophy at the Sorbonne.
Publishes La Conscience de soi.
Publishes La Présence totale.
Publishes Le Mal et la souffrance.
Appointed inspector-general of national education and elected to the Collège de France, where he teaches from 1941 to 1951 (a chair opened with the inaugural lecture L'existence et la valeur).
Publishes Du temps et de l'éternité, volume III of the tetralogy La dialectique de l'éternel présent (whose central volume, De l'Acte, is considered his principal work).
Publishes Introduction à l'ontologie; elected to the Académie des sciences morales et politiques.
Dies in the Lot-et-Garonne (Britannica records Saint-Martin-de-Villeréal as the place of death; French sources give neighboring Parranquet).

philosophers.name: Nietzsche
philosophers.summary: German philosopher and cultural critic, trained as a classical philologist, who published intensely through the 1870s and 1880s. He is known for his radical critiques of traditional European morality, religion and philosophy, and for concepts such as the will to power, the eternal recurrence and the Übermensch. His productive career ended abruptly with the mental collapse of 1889; much of what later circulated under his name was shaped posthumously by his sister Elisabeth's stewardship of the estate.

timeline.label: Born in Röcken, near Lützen in Prussian Saxony, first child of the Lutheran pastor Carl Ludwig Nietzsche. His father died in 1849, and in 1850 the family moved to Naumburg.
Educated on a scholarship at Schulpforta, the boarding school near Naumburg, receiving a rigorous classical training.

A year of theology and philology at Bonn, then follows the philologist Friedrich Ritschl to Leipzig, where he discovers Schopenhauer and, in 1868, meets Richard Wagner; military service with a cavalry regiment is cut short by a serious chest injury.

Called to the chair of classical philology at Basel at 24, before completing the doctorate, on Ritschl's recommendation — the youngest ever appointed to such a post, a superlative recorded here as the SEP's. The sources differ on the appointment's month: the SEP has May, the IEP January, Britannica gives none.
Serves in the Franco-Prussian War as a volunteer medical orderly; contracts dysentery and diphtheria and returns to Basel in permanently weakened health.

Publishes The Birth of Tragedy. The young philologist Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff answers with the pamphlet Zukunftsphilologie!, deriding its method; Erwin Rohde replies in kind and Wagner defends the book in an open letter — a polemic that cost it its standing in the discipline.

The four Untimely Meditations. The winter of 1876–77 is spent in Sorrento with Paul Rée and Malwida von Meysenbug, his first long absence from Basel and the season his distance from Wagner becomes visible. The break with Wagner has no single date: the SEP places it in the mid-1870s, the IEP says 1877, Britannica calls it final by 1878 — a range, recorded as such.
Human, All Too Human, the landmark of the aphoristic 'positivist' middle period.

Resigns the Basel chair on health grounds, with a pension. Britannica dates the resignation 14 June 1879; the IEP writes that he retired in 1878 — the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved. A decade of itinerant writing follows: summers at Sils-Maria in the Engadine, winters in Italian cities and at Nice.
The Gay Science, carrying the first announcement of the 'death of God'; the year also of the intense friendship and breach with Lou Salomé — an episode Britannica's account omits entirely.
Thus Spoke Zarathustra, in four parts; the fourth is printed privately and at first circulates only among a handful of friends.
Beyond Good and Evil (1886) and On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), the central works of the maturity; an expanded second edition of The Gay Science follows in 1887.

The last productive year, largely in Turin: The Case of Wagner is the only one of its books he saw published. Twilight of the Idols appeared in 1889, The Antichrist and Nietzsche contra Wagner in 1895, Ecce Homo only in 1908 — everything after the collapse reached the public through the estate.

Collapses in Turin — the breakdown itself is in every source. The famous horse is not: the SEP and Britannica omit the anecdote entirely, the IEP hedges with 'reportedly', and its sole original source is a 1900 interview with Nietzsche's Turin landlord conducted by an unnamed journalist relaying an unnamed policeman — third-hand, eleven years after the event, with no coachman and no flogging in it. It is recorded here as an attributed tradition, not an established event.

The clinic years and after: Basel, then the Jena asylum under Otto Binswanger, where the contemporaneous diagnosis was dementia paralytica — tertiary syphilis; from 1890 in his mother's care in Naumburg, and from 1897, after her death, in his sister's at the Villa Silberblick in Weimar.

The diagnosis has remained open. Against the syphilis verdict stand named alternatives: a 2008 neurological study proposing CADASIL, Huenemann's 2013 case for a slow-growing retro-orbital meningioma, and frontotemporal dementia; a 2015 survey of the question concludes it is unresolved. The SEP itself endorses the meningioma reading — recorded here as the SEP's position, not as a settled fact.
His sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche founds the Nietzsche-Archiv in Naumburg in 1894 and moves it to Weimar in 1896.

Dies in Weimar — the SEP records a stroke complicated by pneumonia — and is buried beside his father at Röcken. Elisabeth outlived him by thirty-five years, controlling the estate until her death in 1935.

The Will to Power is published — an arrangement of notebook material by Elisabeth and Peter Gast, expanded in 1906. The SEP judges the compilation not well founded in Nietzsche's surviving plans and marred by Elisabeth's editorial hand; the critical Colli–Montinari edition, begun in 1967, dissolved the book back into the notebooks, Montinari concluding that a book called The Will to Power does not exist. Elisabeth's tampering with letters is documented separately; the broader claim that she forged The Will to Power outruns the record and is not made here.

philosophers.name: Leibniz
philosophers.summary: German polymath — philosopher, mathematician, jurist and diplomat — counted among the great rationalists of the seventeenth century. He developed the differential and integral calculus independently of Newton and formulated a metaphysical system centered on the monads and pre-established harmony. He spent most of his career in the service of the House of Hanover.

timeline.label: Born in Leipzig (21 June by the Julian calendar then in use; 1 July by the Gregorian, as Britannica records).
Enters the University of Leipzig, beginning his formation in philosophy and law.
Completes his doctorate in law; the same year he meets Baron von Boineburg, who secures him a position at the court of the Elector of Mainz.
Diplomatic mission in Paris, then the center of European science, with a brief journey to London (1673); he frequents the leading savants of the age.
Lays the foundations of the differential and integral calculus, per Britannica.
Enters the service of the House of Hanover as librarian to Duke Johann Friedrich; on the way, meets Spinoza in Amsterdam (18–21 November).
Writes the Discourse on Metaphysics and begins the correspondence with Arnauld, central expositions of his mature metaphysics.
Publishes the Essays of Theodicy, the only philosophical book he published in his lifetime.
Writes the Monadology and the Principles of Nature and Grace, final syntheses of his system; that year his patron Georg Ludwig becomes George I of England, but Leibniz remains in Hanover.
Dies in Hanover.

philosophers.name: Mário Ferreira dos Santos
philosophers.summary: Brazilian philosopher, translator and journalist, self-taught and deliberately outside the university, who built a system he called 'concrete philosophy' and published it through the 1950s and 1960s as the Enciclopédia de Ciências Filosóficas e Sociais. How many volumes it finally ran to is disputed: 45, 48 and 'more than 50' are all in print, each with a different source and a different way of counting. He translated from German, French and English, passed through São Paulo's anarchist milieu in the mid-1940s, and held no teaching post — 'Nunca ocupei nenhum cargo em nenhuma escola, por princípio', he said of himself in 1976. He fell into obscurity after his death in 1968 and has been republished since the late 1990s by several houses, most visibly É Realizações, whose programme of reissues was run by Olavo de Carvalho until it was reassigned in or before 2018.

timeline.label: Born Mário Dias Ferreira dos Santos in Tietê, in the state of São Paulo, son of Francisco Dias Ferreira dos Santos — a Portuguese from the Porto region who ran the itinerant theatre company Guarany-Brazil and is described as a pioneer of Brazilian cinema. The date descends from Carlo Beraldo's 1969 Enciclopedia Filosofica entry, which reaches this page only as quoted in Brazilian secondary literature; the corresponding Wikidata claim carries no reference at all. Tietê is near-universal, though the Faculdade Dehoniana's 2023 course notice gives 'São Paulo, SP' — an imprecision on an institutional site rather than a rival claim.

The family moves to Pelotas, Rio Grande do Sul, where the father sets up a printing works, a cinema circuit, the Teatro Guarany and the Guarany Films production company; childhood and adolescence are spent there. The account is the UFPB dissertation's, which states in its own note that its entire biographical section comes from the unpublished family monograph written by his daughter and his wife.

Appears as a child in Os Óculos do Vovô, a short directed by his father and held by the Cinemateca Brasileira among the oldest surviving Brazilian films. The filmography record cited for it (ID 001395) reaches this page through a pt.wikipedia footnote and has not been checked against the Cinemateca directly, so the appearance is recorded as unverified.

Educated at the Jesuit Gymnasio, later Colégio Gonzaga, in Pelotas, until the age of eighteen. His atheist and anticlerical father enrolled him there for the quality of the teaching — the origin story he himself gave for his first contact with what he later called 'Filosofia Positiva'. Beraldo's entry confirms the school; the anecdote is the family monograph's.

Reads Law and Social Sciences at the Faculdade de Direito de Porto Alegre, graduating in 1930. His first press article, 'O poeta da luz e da cor', appears in the Diário Popular of Pelotas on 20 July 1928 — the start of a career that runs to some 177 articles in the papers of Pelotas, Porto Alegre and São Paulo. The UFPB dissertation dates the beginning of the press work to 1928; the exact date, the title and the article count come from pt.wikipedia sourced to the family monograph. He supports the Revolution of 1930 as a journalist and then turns on acts of the new government.

Becomes director of the Rio Grande do Sul newspaper A Opinião Pública, and marries; two daughters follow, Yolanda and Nadiejda. The chain here is family testimony and is not independently corroborated. The sources also carry a name collision they do not resolve — Yolanda Duro Lhullier is given both as his mother and as his wife — and it is recorded here rather than smoothed away.

Arrested, reportedly for encouraging worker strikes, and released through the intervention of General Flores da Cunha and the Pelotas mayor Py Crespo, losing the newspaper directorship. He published his own account, 'PORQUE FUI DETIDO', in A Opinião Pública of 19 December 1930 — a datable primary document, located through a pt.wikipedia footnote and not seen here.
A documented gap. No source consulted for this page accounts for these eight years, and pt.wikipedia says as much explicitly. Recorded as unknown rather than filled in from the surrounding narrative.

Resumes press work — Clímax in Pelotas, Movimento and the Diário de Notícias in Porto Alegre. After his father's death the family firm, Empresa Xavier & Santos, the largest cinema chain in southern Brazil and by then under his direction, goes bankrupt in 1941.

Contracted by the Livraria do Globo in Porto Alegre to translate Nietzsche, Pascal, Amiel and Balzac, all from the originals. Globo then refuses a philosophical essay of his own, on the advice of a reader who held that Brazilians would not read philosophy — the stated trigger for his departure, and an account that comes from the family monograph. The years of the individual Nietzsche translations are the weakest point in this chronology: the UFPel dissertation that would fix them returns 403 from this session and has no Wayback snapshot.

Moves to São Paulo. The year is not settled and both are recorded: pt.wikipedia gives 1945, a UFPel-adjacent account has him arriving around 1944 carrying his translation of the Vontade de Potência from the Globo period, and the UFPB dissertation gives no year at all. In São Paulo he translates for Editora Flama (Whitman, Benjamin Constant, Goethe), then directs the editorial section of Editora e Distribuidora Sagitário, publishing work of his own under pseudonyms, and later works in the rare-books section of the Livraria Ritz.

Anarchist militancy in São Paulo: active at the Centro de Cultura Social, one of the city's principal anarchist nuclei, where he lectures and meets Jaime Cubero in 1945. At Sagitário he translates Rudolf Rocker — the one documented translation of the anarchist period. Two texts circulate in libertarian periodicals: Teses da Existência e da Inexistência de Deus, under the name Charles Duclos (Sagitário, 1946), and Análise Dialética do Marxismo. He is read and cited by Edgard Leuenroth and by Cubero, and is one of the few Brazilian students of Christian anarchism. No evidence was found that he ever translated Stirner: the specialist survey of Portuguese Stirner translations does not mention him, and the documented Portuguese versions of Der Einzige are by other hands.

Logos is three things, and no source consulted reconciles them. pt.wikipedia has an Instituto Cultural Logos founded in 1947, a teaching institute giving in-person and correspondence courses in Portuguese, history, geography, the sciences, mathematics, psychology, philosophy, logic, dialectic and 'cosmovisão'. The UFPB dissertation has the Livraria e Editora Logos Ltda., the publishing house, founded in 1953, whose first titles are write-ups of oratory courses heavily attended by politicians and lawyers — Curso de Oratória e Retórica, Práticas de Oratória, Técnica do Discurso Moderno. pt.wikipedia also refers to a 'Logos S.A.' founded after 1952. These are plausibly three stages of one venture; they are recorded as three because nothing consulted joins them. From 1947 he says he gave himself entirely to philosophy, teaching private pupils and small informal groups.
Compiles the cheap-format collection 'Cultura para Milhões' for Editora Edigraf — newsprint, no illustrations, deliberately low-cost, to widen access.

Filosofia e Cosmovisão, later designated volume 1 of the Enciclopédia de Ciências Filosóficas e Sociais, opens the project, and the systematic introductions follow across the branches: Lógica e Dialética (1953), Psicologia (1953), Teoria do Conhecimento (1954), Ontologia e Cosmologia (1954), Tratado de Simbólica (1956), Filosofia da Crise (1956), O Homem Perante o Infinito (1956) and Noologia Geral (1956). These years are the FAJE monograph's, and this is the messiest area in the record. For the first volume alone: 1952 under the Edanee imprint in the FAJE narrative and pt.wikipedia's prose; 1954 under Logos in pt.wikipedia's own bibliography, which contradicts its prose; 1955 under Logos on the scanned copy circulating online. Reprints issued without new-edition statements, and the retroactive renumbering of earlier books into the encyclopedia sequence, are the likely causes; the rule applied here is to cite the imprint one can actually see and say which copy it is.

The first twelve volumes appear. Distributors decline to carry them for want of demand, so he pioneers door-to-door book sales on credit — venda a crediário — in Brazil, successfully enough that he has to take premises able to receive sales representatives arriving from across the country. The anecdote comes through the family monograph.

Filosofia Concreta, the tenth work of the series and the one at which, in the standard academic reading, he passes from commentator and essayist to philosopher. The date is the FAJE monograph's; pt.wikipedia's work-list gives 1956 and the scanned Logos tomes I–III give 1961.

How large the Enciclopédia de Ciências Filosóficas e Sociais finally was is disputed, and the figures are not noise: they turn on whether multi-tome works are counted once or severally, and on whether the Matese-imprint books count as encyclopedia volumes at all. Beraldo's 1969 entry gives 45 volumes 'in less than fifteen years', and is the origin of the figure most often repeated without attribution; Carlos Eduardo de Carvalho Vargas (Revista Nures, PUC-SP, 2007) gives 48, the last of them titled Deus; Miriam Dornas Gomes Pereira (FAJE, 2019) gives 'more than 50'; and catalogue copy circulates a fourth figure, '45 planned', which is a different claim again. The range is reported with each figure's source; none of them is chosen here.

Founds Editora Matese, which issues classics, the Matese series and the long-planned Dicionário de Filosofia e Ciências Culturais in four volumes (1963). The late books follow: A Invasão Vertical dos Bárbaros and A Sabedoria dos Princípios, which opens the Matese series, both 1967, with A Sabedoria da Unidade also in 1967 and A Sabedoria do Ser e do Nada in 1968.

Dies, with very nearly the whole encyclopedia published in his lifetime. The date is solid — consistent across every source and present in Beraldo's 1969 entry. The particulars are not. That he died in São Paulo, of cardiovascular disease, and was buried in the Cemitério do Araçá rests on three Wikidata claims (P570, P20, P119), each of which carries zero references when the entity JSON is checked, and on a Find a Grave memorial that returns 403 to every client tried here. Place, cause and burial are therefore recorded as unverified.

Stanislavs Ladusãns publishes Rumos da filosofia atual no Brasil: em auto-retratos, whose pages 407–409 carry Ferreira dos Santos's own self-portrait and the much-quoted line 'Nunca ocupei nenhum cargo em nenhuma escola, por princípio' — I have never held any post in any school, on principle. Ladusãns places him among the leading Brazilian philosophers of the first half of the century, beside Flusser, Cruz Costa and Lima Vaz. The book is print-only and could not be obtained here, so the quotation is carried at second hand. The claim, widely circulated, that he taught philosophy of science at the USP Escola Politécnica and philosophy of communication at the Escola Superior de Cinema and the Escola de Arte Dramática in the 1960s is deliberately absent from this timeline: every occurrence traced runs back to movement and fan sites rather than to a USP institutional record, and this sentence of his own contradicts it.

Academic reception, thin and late. Wadson Machado Neto's 1988 UFJF master's thesis is repeatedly named as the first academic study; later work includes Vargas (PUC-SP, 2007), Roger Moura dos Santos (UFPB, 2016), Elvis Amsterdã (UFSC, 2019), Pereira (FAJE, 2019) and Braga (Ítaca/UFRJ, 2024). João Cezar de Castro Rocha, in his preface to the 2017 Filosofia da Crise, attributes the long neglect partly to the 1950s turn toward university-based philosophical research, against which Ferreira dos Santos's autodidactism read as illegitimate — his explanation, offered in a book of the revival, and recorded as such.

Scattered posthumous republication, and not by one house: O Apocalipse de São João (Editorial Cone Sul, 1998), O Um e o Múltiplo em Platão and Pitágoras e o Tema do Número reissued by IBRASA (2000 and 2001), and Cristianismo, a Religião do Homem by the university press EDUSC (2003). In 2001 É Realizações published A Sabedoria das Leis Eternas, the earliest of its Ferreira dos Santos titles that can be dated here, 'com introdução, edição e notas de Olavo de Carvalho'. É Realizações had been founded in 2000 out of a cultural space Edson Manoel de Oliveira Filho had run since 1995, which hosted Olavo de Carvalho's courses from 1996–97.

The systematic É Realizações reissues: Tratado de Simbólica (2007), Filosofia Concreta (2009), A Invasão Vertical dos Bárbaros (2012), Filosofia e Cosmovisão (2015, reprinted 2018), Filosofia da Crise (2017, with prefaces by Hans Ulrich Gumbrecht and João Cezar de Castro Rocha) and Homens da Tarde (2019); Lógica e Dialética came from PAULUS in 2007. These years are taken from third-party bibliographic and retail records: the publisher's own site refuses connections from this session, so its catalogue could not be checked. The reissues were accompanied by a layer of sympathetic profiles in the Brazilian press and in cultural blogs, which repeat the encyclopedia figure and the biography without attribution; they are cited here as evidence of the rediscovery discourse and not as sources for anything in it.

The revival's authorship is itself contested, and is attributed here rather than asserted. Francisco Escorsim reports in Gazeta do Povo that the É Realizações programme of Ferreira dos Santos republication, until then managed by Olavo de Carvalho, had been reassigned, producing 'significant changes in editorial treatment' and few new titles since. It is the one independent press account of the revival's internal history, and it is why no version of 'É Realizações rescued Mário Ferreira dos Santos' is stated on this page: that is a claim with a history behind it.

Elvis Amsterdã's Vida e Obra de Mário Ferreira dos Santos: Uma Introdução (Curitiba: Editora Danúbio, 100 pp.) — the first book-length biographical study, with a biographical chronology, photographs and unpublished documents in an appendix, reviewed in the Revista Filosófica de Coimbra the following year. It is known to this page only through that review, and it is the book to read before any of the disagreements recorded above is closed.

philosophers.name: Santo Agostinho
philosophers.summary: Bishop of Hippo and one of the most influential Christian thinkers of all time, the bridge between ancient philosophy and medieval thought. A professor of rhetoric converted to ascetic Christianity in 386, he left more than five million words of surviving writings, among them the Confessions and The City of God.

timeline.label: Born in Thagaste, in Roman Africa (present-day Souk Ahras, Algeria), son of Monica, a devout Christian, and Patricius, baptized only on his deathbed.
Becomes a 'hearer' (auditor) of Manichaeism, the dualist religion of Persian origin, to which he remains attached for about a decade.
Moves to Italy and takes up in Milan, then capital of the Western Empire, the public post of professor of rhetoric and panegyrist of the imperial court (the SEP dates the move to Milan to 383).
Converts to ascetic Christianity and renounces the chair of rhetoric and his career prospects.
At the rural retreat of Cassiciacum, near Milan, writes his first philosophical dialogues (Contra Academicos, De beata vita, De ordine).
Baptized by Ambrose in Milan; on the return to Africa, his mother dies at Ostia (388).
Ordained a priest at Hippo Regius (present-day Annaba, Algeria), apparently against his own wishes.
Becomes bishop of Hippo — Britannica gives 395 or 396; the SEP, about 396.
Writes the Confessions, 'philosophy in autobiography' — the SEP dates the work to c. 396–400; Britannica, to c. 400.
Writes The City of God, his great work of the theology of history, begun after the sack of Rome.
Dies at Hippo Regius, aged 75.

philosophers.name: Eric Voegelin
philosophers.summary: German-American political philosopher, formed in Vienna, who fled Nazism in 1938 and made his career in the United States and Munich. He sought a comprehensive philosophy of man, society and history, and became known for his analysis of modern political movements as 'gnosticism'. His principal works include The New Science of Politics and the Order and History series.

timeline.label: Born in Cologne, Germany; the family later moves to Vienna, where he receives his entire formation.
Obtains the habilitation and begins teaching at the University of Vienna (Britannica records his teaching at the Law Faculty from 1929 to 1938).
Publishes two books critically analyzing racism and race ideas, which set him against Nazism.
Publishes Der autoritäre Staat (The Authoritarian State).
After the Anschluss, flees Austria with his wife, passing through Switzerland before emigrating to the United States.
Professor at Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge; becomes a US citizen in 1944.
Publishes The New Science of Politics, the work that projects him into the American intellectual debate.
Publishes the first three volumes of Order and History; volume 4 appears in 1974 and the posthumous volume 5 in 1987.
Takes up in Munich the former chair of Max Weber in political science at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität.
Publishes Anamnesis: Zur Theorie der Geschichte und Politik, central to his philosophy of consciousness.
Returns to the United States as senior research fellow at the Hoover Institution, Stanford University.
Dies at Stanford, California.

philosophers.name: Husserl
philosophers.summary: A mathematician by training and the founder of phenomenology, the movement that marked all of twentieth-century continental philosophy. He made his career at Halle, Göttingen and Freiburg, where Heidegger succeeded him. Of Jewish origin, he spent his last years excluded from German university life under the Nazi regime.

readings.claim: Named second in his twentieth-century canon, after Lavelle: what Husserl gave humanity, he says, cannot yet be measured, and everything of his he studies still holds seeds for centuries to come. The machine transcription writes the name 'Russel' throughout — one of the three documented traps in this corpus.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 04 — Aristotle

timeline.label: Born in Proßnitz, Moravia, then in the Austrian Empire (present-day Prostějov, Czechia).
Takes his doctorate in mathematics in Vienna with a thesis on the calculus of variations; works briefly as Weierstrass's assistant in Berlin.
Privatdozent at the University of Halle for fourteen years; in 1891 publishes his first book, Philosophy of Arithmetic.
Publishes the Logical Investigations, the founding work of phenomenology.
Professor at Göttingen (extraordinarius from 1901, ordinarius from 1906), a position secured by the success of the Investigations.
Publishes Ideas for a Pure Phenomenology (Ideas I), the transcendental turn of his thought.
Takes the chair of philosophy at Freiburg, succeeding the neo-Kantian Heinrich Rickert; Edith Stein becomes his assistant.
Retires at Freiburg, succeeded by Heidegger; shortly afterwards delivers in Paris the lectures that would become the Cartesian Meditations.

With the arrival of Nazism, suffers the exclusion imposed on Jews in Germany — in a letter of 4 May 1933 he speaks of the erection of a 'spiritual ghetto' in which he and his children were being enclosed.
Publishes (in part) The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology, developed from lectures in Vienna and Prague.
Dies in Freiburg im Breisgau.

philosophers.name: Heidegger
philosophers.summary: A central figure of twentieth-century European philosophy, author of Being and Time (1927) and renewer of the question of the meaning of being. Husserl's disciple and successor at Freiburg, he influenced existentialism, hermeneutics and deconstruction. His involvement with Nazism — the 1933–34 rectorate and party membership until 1945 — remains an object of controversy.

timeline.label: Born in Messkirch, in the Black Forest region of Germany.
Becomes associate professor at the University of Marburg, where he teaches ontology, logic and the history of philosophy until 1928.
Publishes Being and Time, his greatest work, and is promoted to full professor at Marburg.
Appointed to the Freiburg chair previously held by Rickert and by Husserl, whose successor he becomes.
Elected rector of the University of Freiburg after Hitler's seizure of power; joins the Nazi Party on 1 May and conducts the 'alignment' (Gleichschaltung) of the university.
Resigns the rectorate, but remains a party member until the end of the regime.
Delivers the great lecture courses on Nietzsche, later collected in book form; in the 1930s–40s he also lectures on Hölderlin, Schelling, Hegel and the pre-Socratics.
After Germany's surrender and the denazification hearings, the French military government bans him from all teaching and university activity.
The teaching ban is lifted, allowing him to assume emeritus status at Freiburg.
Publishes Holzwege (Off the Beaten Track), collecting essays from 1935–1946.
Dies in Freiburg im Breisgau.

philosophers.name: Frithjof Schuon
philosophers.summary: Swiss-German writer and metaphysician, the leading exponent of the perennialist (Traditionalist) school in the twentieth century alongside René Guénon and Ananda Coomaraswamy. Initiated into Sufism in Algeria in 1933, he directed from Europe — and, after 1980, from Bloomington, Indiana — the order that became known as the Maryamiyya, and wrote dozens of books on metaphysics, comparative religion and sacred art. The accounts of his life here follow chiefly his estate's site and the historian of Traditionalism Mark Sedgwick.

timeline.label: Born in Basel, Switzerland, son of a German violinist.
After his father's death, moves with his mother to Mulhouse, in French Alsace.
Settles in Paris, where he works and deepens his study of Arabic and of Eastern doctrines.

Travels to Mostaganem, Algeria, enters Islam and spends about four months at the zawiya of the Sufi shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi, from whom he receives initiation (the date per the estate's site; other reconstructions place the departure from Europe in late 1932).
Publishes his first book, in German: Leitgedanken zur Urbesinnung (Primordial Meditation).
Settles in Lausanne, Switzerland, his base for nearly four decades.
Publishes De l'Unité transcendante des religions, his first and best-known book in French, the classic formulation of the perennialist thesis.
Marries Catherine Feer; obtains Swiss citizenship shortly afterwards.
Travels to the American West at the invitation of Indigenous friends; on the 1959 visit he is adopted by the Sioux (and, in 1984, by the Crow).
Publishes mature works such as Logic and Transcendence, Form and Substance in the Religions and Esoterism as Principle and as Way.

Emigrates with his wife to the United States, settling in Bloomington, Indiana, near a community of disciples; in the first years there publishes From the Divine to the Human, To Have a Center and Roots of the Human Condition.

Becomes the target, in Bloomington, of accusations taken to a grand jury on the complaints of a former disciple; the prosecution dropped the charges shortly afterwards — an episode documented by the historian Mark Sedgwick in Against the Modern World (2004) and discussed on his academic blog.
Dies in Bloomington, Indiana.

philosophers.name: Ortega y Gasset
philosophers.summary: Spanish philosopher, essayist and intellectual leader, formed in German neo-Kantianism and creator of 'vital reason' ('I am I and my circumstance'). Professor of metaphysics in Madrid and founder of the Revista de Occidente, he became world-famous with The Revolt of the Masses. He left Spain with the Civil War and returned after the Second World War.

timeline.label: Born in Madrid, into a family tied to liberal journalism.
Studies in Germany — Leipzig, Berlin and, decisively, Marburg, under neo-Kantianism — before returning to Madrid.
Wins the competition (8 October) for the chair of metaphysics at the Central University of Madrid, vacant since the death of Nicolás Salmerón.
Publishes Meditaciones del Quijote, where the formula 'I am I and my circumstance' appears.
Publishes España invertebrada — the SEP dates the book to 1921; Britannica, to 1922.
Founds the Revista de Occidente, the leading organ of intellectual renewal in the Spain of the period.
Publishes La rebelión de las masas, his most famous work — Britannica dates it to 1929 (as a series of articles); the SEP records the book in 1930.
Becomes one of the first members of the Constituent Cortes of the Second Spanish Republic.
With the outbreak of the Civil War, leaves Spain; lives in Europe and Argentina, returning at the end of the Second World War (Britannica describes the period as voluntary exile).

Founds in Madrid, with his disciple Julián Marías, the Instituto de Humanidades — he never resumed his university chair, and the government restricts the institute's activities until its closure in 1950.
Dies in Madrid.

philosophers.name: Dante Alighieri
philosophers.fullName: Dante Alighieri (Durante di Alighiero degli Alighieri)
philosophers.summary: Poet, political thinker and 'father of the Italian language', author of the Divine Comedy, the poetic synthesis of medieval culture. He took an active part in the civic life of Florence until his condemnation to exile in 1302, and wrote in banishment his great prose works and the poem that immortalized him. He died in Ravenna in 1321.

timeline.label: Born in Florence — if he was indeed born under Gemini, as the Paradiso suggests, the birthday would fall between mid-May and mid-June (Britannica records c. 21 May–20 June).
By the testimony of his own writings, meets at age nine Beatrice Portinari, whom after her death (1290) he will invoke as the inspiration of his poetic vision.
Marries and starts a family; from then on takes part in Florence's cultural and civic life, serves as a soldier and holds various political offices.
Composes the Vita nuova, the prosimetrum in praise of Beatrice.
Condemned and exiled from Florence in the struggle between Guelph factions; he will never return to the city.
Writes the Convivio, abandoned with only four of the projected treatises, and De vulgari eloquentia, on the illustrious vernacular.
Composes the Divine Comedy (Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso), per Britannica's dating.
In the years of the expedition of Henry VII of Luxembourg, crowned emperor in 1312, becomes an impassioned propagandist of universal empire.
Writes the Monarchia, the Latin treatise on the necessity of an imperial power independent of the Church — its dating is disputed; the SEP considers composition after 1314 probable.
Moves from Verona (the court of Cangrande della Scala) to Ravenna, where he completes the Paradiso.
Dies in Ravenna — Britannica records the date as 13/14 September.

philosophers.name: Fílon de Alexandria
philosophers.summary: Hellenistic Jewish philosopher of Alexandria, who read the Pentateuch allegorically and in Greek philosophical terms, and whose Logos became a load-bearing idea for later Christian theology. Almost nothing in his life is securely dated: one embassy anchors the whole biography, and the standard references disagree about his birth by thirty years.

timeline.label: Born in Alexandria. No source claims precision and the most recent decline to give a year at all: the Catholic Encyclopedia says c. 25 BCE, the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy c. 20, Britannica 15–10, and the Stanford Encyclopedia states that it is impossible to date and that the consensus is only that he lived between the end of the first century BCE and the middle of the first century CE. Every one of those figures is back-calculated from a single detail — that he describes himself as an old man at the time of the embassy.

Born into the wealthiest Jewish family in Alexandria. His brother Alexander held the office of alabarch, a senior fiscal post carrying citizenship privileges most Alexandrian Jews were denied. His nephew Tiberius Julius Alexander left Judaism, became prefect of Egypt and served as Titus's second-in-command at the siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE.

Riots against the Jews of Alexandria, which the Stanford Encyclopedia calls the first major pogrom in Jewish history: imperial images installed in the synagogues, the Jewish population confined to the Delta district, members of the council scourged. Philo's own account is In Flaccum. The reconstruction is contested — Gambetti argues the trigger was the enforcement of residential decrees rather than religious hostility, which her reviewer disputes on the ground that the Delta district is never named in Philo's text.

THE ONE SECURELY DATED EVENT OF HIS LIFE. He goes to Rome at the head of the Alexandrian Jewish embassy to Gaius (Caligula), and is prevented from putting his case. Britannica states it plainly as the single identifiable event; Josephus independently attests his leading of the delegation, and Eusebius calls him the chief of the embassy. Everything else in this timeline — his birth, his death, the order in which he wrote — is positioned relative to it.

Gaius is assassinated. The embassy was one book of a five-book work, of which only In Flaccum and the Legatio ad Gaium survive; the lost 'palinode' told of Gaius's fall and so must have been written after this date.

Death, undated. Britannica gives 45–50; the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives c. 40, which cannot be right if he wrote about the fall of Gaius; the Stanford Encyclopedia gives only the middle of the first century.

The corpus is conventionally divided into five groups — the Allegorical Commentary (39 treatises), the Exposition of the Law (12), the Questions and Answers on Genesis and Exodus (6 surviving of an original 12), four historical and apologetic works, and five philosophical ones. The division is Massebiau's and Cohn's, of 1889 and 1899, not Philo's own.

No agreed chronology of the works existed until 2018. Niehoff then moved De opificio mundi from the head of the corpus to the late work and split the writing at the Roman embassy: an early Alexandrian and Platonic phase in the Allegorical Commentary, a later Stoic and Roman one in the Exposition. Her reviewer calls the evidence very strong while suggesting the phases may be less cleanly separable than the argument needs.

The corpus reaches Caesarea, the city from which it was transmitted. Its survival is the paradox the Stanford Encyclopedia states outright: his work was ignored by Jews and saved by Christians, some of whom believed he had been one. Eusebius reports the legend that he met Peter in Rome and reads his account of the Therapeutae as a description of Christian ascetics. Runia's account of transmission through Origen's Caesarean volumes is standard; his reviewer thinks the route was probably less exclusive than that.

readings.claim: He puts Philo at the head of allegorical interpretation and says a good part of the technique was already there before Christianity — Philo working only from the Old Testament and the Greek material, with no contact with Christianity that his writings show. Against the charge that the readings are artificial, a contrivance to make two things fit, his answer is that the first person to do anything never does it properly: the technique had to be deepened, criticised and elaborated, and full mastery of it appears only with Hugh of St Victor and Aquinas.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08 — the advent of Christianity

readings.claim: He dates Philo to roughly forty years before Christ and forty after — which is earlier than any of the standard references, whose range for the birth runs from 25 to 10 BCE. Recorded as his figure, not corrected in his mouth.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

readings.claim: Historians with good philosophical training but no command of symbolic language, he says, see contradictions in Philo that are not there — for instance the charge that he confuses the angelic hierarchies with the hierarchy of ideas. On his reading these are not rival theories: the eternal ideas are the content of the divine intelligence, the plan of creation, while the angelic hierarchies are the mode in which divine action operates. The plan and the method of building are different things.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

readings.claim: He credits Philo with explicitly identifying Plato's supreme good with Aristotle's unmoved first mover — not two antagonistic principles but one, described in moral language and in metaphysical language. He treats this as a real philosophical achievement rather than a syncretism.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

readings.claim: Why a great philosopher appears in a period he regards as one of philosophical decadence: Philo belonged to another community and so was spared the collective disorientation that followed the fall of the polis — he had the Law of Moses under his arm — while holding a problem that could actually be posed and worked, the relation between Jewish and Greek wisdom.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

readings.claim: On Philo's claim that the Jewish tradition came first, he splits the question. Read historically it is simply wrong — there is no evidence any disciple of Moses taught in Greece, and he says so flatly. Read as ontological priority it is not absurd: the knowledge of God is prior to the knowledge of sensible reality, so a tradition concentrated on God holds the rest implicitly, compacted in mythopoetic language.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

readings.claim: The criticism is as sharp as the praise, and this entry keeps both. Philo did not read Hebrew and knew the Mosaic doctrine only through the Septuagint, so the Judaism he defends is, in his phrase, somewhat doubtful — a philosopher defending what was left of Judaism in his own head rather than an authorised spokesman for its orthodoxy. His grasp of the Greek philosophers he judges deficient too: Philo mixes Stoics with Platonists and attributes to one what belongs to the other.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

readings.claim: He makes Philo the model for a problem that recurs inside Christianity: Clement of Alexandria saw between Greek philosophy and the new revelation the same link of continuity Philo had seen between the old Jewish revelation and Greek philosophy — philosophy as the tutor that leads to Christ. He adds that for a situation like Philo's to arise within Christianity, a great deal of time had to pass first, since the doctrine was still rudimentary and the Greco-Roman legacy not yet sufficiently known.
readings.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 08

philosophers.name: René Girard
philosophers.summary: French-American literary critic, anthropologist and philosopher of religion; professor at Stanford from 1981 and a member of the Académie française from 2005. He is known for mimetic theory: desire is borrowed from a model rather than being autonomous, the rivalry it produces drives collective violence, and archaic societies discharged that violence through a scapegoat mechanism which he read the Gospels as exposing. Michel Serres, replying to his reception speech in 2005, called him 'the new Darwin of the human sciences' — a superlative recorded here as Serres's, spoken in a ceremony of praise.

timeline.label: Born in Avignon as René Noël Théophile Girard, son of Joseph Girard (1881–1962), archiviste-paléographe of the École nationale des chartes, curator of the Musée Calvet from 1906 to 1949 and thereafter of the Palais des Papes, and of Marie-Thérèse de Loye Fabre (1893–1967). The birth date is one of the few points on which every source consulted agrees: the Académie française, Britannica, the IEP, COV&R and Stanford's own memorial resolution all give it.

Graduates from the École nationale des chartes in 1947 as archiviste-paléographe, with a thesis on private life in Avignon in the second half of the fifteenth century; emigrates to the United States the same year and teaches at Indiana University Bloomington until 1953, taking a doctorate in history there in 1950 with a dissertation on American opinion of France, 1940–1943. The year he entered the École des chartes is given by no source consulted here and is left unstated rather than guessed; the school's published Positions des thèses for 1947 would settle it.

Marries Martha McCullough; three children follow, Martin, Daniel and Mary. The year is disputed and is recorded rather than resolved: Britannica gives 1951, and Stanford Magazine's 'sixty-four years of marriage' counted back from his death agrees with it, while Wikipedia gives 1952. 1951 is the date used here.

Teaches at Duke University and then at Bryn Mawr College. The sources do not divide the window consistently between the two, so it is given as one approximate span rather than split into two dated appointments.

First period at Johns Hopkins, where he is made full professor in 1961. He held two Guggenheim Fellowships: COV&R and the Académie française both describe him as a two-time fellow, but neither names the years. The years 1959 and 1966 circulate from Wikipedia and are confirmed by neither, so they are carried here as unverified rather than stated.

The conversion, narrated here as his own account rather than as an established chronology. Girard told interviewers that an 'intellectual conversion' came in the autumn of 1958, while he was writing the twelfth chapter of his first book, accompanied by quasi-mystical experiences on the Pennsylvania Railroad, and that he rewrote the book's conclusion afterwards; a religious conversion followed during Lent 1959 and was sealed when a melanoma scare was cleared on Holy Wednesday, which in 1959 fell on 25 March. The reference works decline to date any of it: Britannica and the IEP say only that he converted while reading Dostoevsky, without a year, and Wikipedia offers 'c. 1959–1961'. The dates here come from his own interviews and from Cynthia Haven's biography, which itself rests on his retelling.

Mensonge romantique et vérité romanesque (Grasset), the book that introduced mimetic desire through readings of Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust and Dostoevsky. The English translation by Yvonne Freccero, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel, appeared from the Johns Hopkins Press in 1965 — the date in the publisher's own catalogue and in library records. Stanford Magazine and Wikipedia give 1966; 1965 is used here.

'The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man', the Johns Hopkins symposium Girard convened with Richard Macksey and Eugenio Donato to introduce French structuralism to American universities. Girard issued the invitations, among them to Jacques Lacan and to Jacques Derrida, whose paper 'La structure, le signe et le jeu dans le discours des sciences humaines' was delivered on 21 October 1966 and is conventionally dated as the arrival of post-structuralism in America — at a conference convened to promote structuralism. The proceedings appeared in 1970 as The Structuralist Controversy, and the symposium audio was digitised by the Sheridan Libraries in 2023.

At the State University of New York at Buffalo. The span is not agreed: the widely copied account has him holding a distinguished professorship from 1971, and other accounts close the period in 1975. It is recorded as an approximate span with the disagreement left standing.

La Violence et le sacré (Grasset), which took a prize of the Académie française; the English Violence and the Sacred, translated by Patrick Gregory, followed from Johns Hopkins University Press in 1977. It is the book that carried the scapegoat mechanism out of literary criticism and into anthropology and the study of religion, and the one on which the disciplinary objections to his method concentrate.

Returns to Johns Hopkins as John M. Beall Professor of the Humanities. In 1978 he publishes Des choses cachées depuis la fondation du monde (Grasset), a book-length dialogue with the psychiatrist Jean-Michel Oughourlian and Guy Lefort in which the reading of the Gospels as the disclosure of the victim mechanism is set out; the English Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World appeared from Stanford University Press in 1987.

At Stanford as the inaugural Andrew B. Hammond Professor of French Language, Literature and Civilization, until his retirement as emeritus in 1995. Stanford's memorial resolution dates the appointment to 1981 and rene-girard.fr to 1980; the university's own record is followed here. The books of these years are Le Bouc émissaire (1982; English The Scapegoat, Johns Hopkins, 1986, trans. Freccero) and La Route antique des hommes pervers (1985; English Job, the Victim of His People, 1987).

Two foundings in one year. In March the Colloquium on Violence & Religion is established at Stanford by James Williams, Charles Mabee and Robert Hamerton-Kelly; it is formally constituted in 1991 with Girard as honorary chair, Raymund Schwager as president and Wolfgang Palaver editing its bulletin, and it publishes the journal Contagion — the association's own account of its beginnings is the only detailed one, and is written from inside. The same year Shakespeare : les feux de l'envie (Grasset), written in English but published in French first, takes the Prix Médicis essai. The publisher's record dates the prize 1990 and Wikipedia 1991; 1990 is used here. The English A Theater of Envy followed from Oxford University Press in 1991.

Je vois Satan tomber comme l'éclair (1999; English I See Satan Fall Like Lightning, Orbis, 2001), the most directly theological of the books, and Les Origines de la culture (2004), a set of interviews which took the Prix Aujourd'hui.

The Rio de Janeiro visit — the point at which this chronology's two subjects meet, and attested only through the Olavo de Carvalho network. A lecture and round table at the auditorium of the Faculdade da Cidade / UniverCidade on 17 November, and an interview at the Hotel Glória the next day, conducted by Pedro Sette Câmara and Alvaro Velloso de Carvalho with Olavo de Carvalho taking part, published on 19 November 2000. No independent Brazilian press record of the visit was found in Folha, Estadão, O Globo or the Jornal do Brasil; olavodecarvalho.org now serves a parked retail template and oindividuo.com returns 503, and the Internet Archive's availability API answered 429 to every request from this session, so no snapshot of either page could be checked in either direction. The only reachable text is an unattributed blog reproduction. Olavo refers to the meeting in the COF transcriptions — aula 18, 18 August 2009, a reviewed file: 'Quando o René Girard esteve no Rio de Janeiro, eu lhe perguntei isso' — which corroborates that a meeting took place but is itself part of the same network. Recorded as attributed, not as established.

Elected to the Académie française on 17 March 2005 to fauteuil 37, succeeding the Dominican Ambroise-Marie Carré, on the sponsorship of Jacqueline de Romilly and Marc Fumaroli; received under the Coupole on 15 December 2005, with the reply delivered by Michel Serres. Serres's speech is the origin of the tag 'the new Darwin of the human sciences' — his phrase, in a ceremony whose genre is praise, and not a judgement this page makes. The reception is sometimes dated 2006; the Académie's own notice puts it on 15 December 2005.

Honours, a last book and an institution. The Dr Leopold Lucas Prize (Tübingen) in 2006 and the Modern Language Association's Award for Lifetime Scholarly Achievement in 2008, alongside honorary doctorates from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (1985), UFSIA Antwerp (1995), Padua (2001), Montréal (2004) and St Andrews (2008), and the Légion d'honneur as chevalier. In October 2007 Achever Clausewitz, his book-length conversation with Benoît Chantre, appeared from Carnets Nord; the English Battling to the End is dated 2009 in Stanford's obituary and 2010 by Stanford Magazine, and that discrepancy is left open here. 2007 is also the year Imitatio was founded to fund and propagate mimetic theory — a project of Peter Thiel's Thiel Foundation, set up with Robert Hamerton-Kelly, recorded here from a third-party account rather than from Imitatio's own.

Dies at his home on the Stanford campus, aged 91; the Académie française posted its death notice the next day. He was survived by Martha and their three children, and Stanford held a memorial on 19 January 2016. The standard obituaries — the Stanford Report of 4 November 2015, Quentin Hardy in the New York Times of 11 November 2015 and Jean Birnbaum in Le Monde of 5 November 2015 — exist but were unreachable from this session (Cloudflare, 403 and a paywall respectively), and are therefore not cited.

doctrines.note: Concepts Olavo de Carvalho named and taught as his own. This section is EXPOSITION, not endorsement: each entry says what he claimed, where he expounded it and when, and whom he credited. The project takes no view on whether any of it is true, exactly as the philosopher pages record his readings without adjudicating them. Summaries are the project's own words; his formulations are paraphrased rather than reproduced, and the few terms of art quoted are his coinages. Where a lecture date is unverified the entry says so, and where he revised a doctrine the revision is shown rather than smoothed into a single version.
doctrines.sourceNote: Drawn from the community transcription corpus of the course (585 lectures) and the video collection. A third of the fullest expositions sit in files the transcription project has not reviewed and that carry no date at all, so some entries below cite an undated lecture — that is a property of the corpus, not an omission here. The panel is a work in progress and is reviewed against the transcripts as new material lands (ADR-0005): an entry's absence is not evidence that he had no such doctrine, and entries already here are corrected when the corpus contradicts them.

items.claim: A scheme of twelve demands that structure a human life, from taking possession of one's own body to standing before eternity. Each layer is a distinct kind of interest that can organise a person's whole existence, and he holds that most adults halt at the eighth, the crisis of maturity.
items.origin: Built in his Astrocaracterologia course (1990–92) from the twelve houses of the zodiac, taken as an ideal developmental circuit and grafted onto Szondi's drive psychology — which he said lacked any biographical dimension. He states three times that the scheme does not depend on astrology: he devised it to isolate precisely what a horoscope cannot describe.
items.revision: Presented as an evolutionary sequence in 2010 and 2014, then corrected in a later lecture: it is not an ideal development but the real structure of human existence, with all twelve demands pressing at once. He then distinguished the layer a person occupies from the stage that weighs on them. The diagram shows twelve simultaneous demands for that reason.

items.title: The twelve layers of personality
items.lineageNote: What moves a person between layers, in the class devoted to the scheme, is symbolic material: someone with no culture to think with cannot articulate what the crisis of maturity is doing to them, and so cannot pass out of it — the effort of articulation is itself what carries them across. He puts the intellectual personality on the far side of that crisis, and adds that what began as one person's private trouble becomes useful to others precisely because articulating it gives voice to people who could not. That class is also the strongest evidence for his repeated insistence that the scheme does not depend on astrology: across its full length neither astrology, nor the zodiac, nor Szondi is mentioned once.

items.claim: Beneath perception, memory and theory there is a prior, non-representational cognition that consists in reality simply being present to the knower. He calls it the most exact form of knowledge precisely because it cannot be turned into a thought one possesses. Its work is to explain how anyone ever corrects a framework from inside it: without it, he argues, a powerful philosophy would hypnotise its adherents completely and no school could revise itself.

items.title: Cognitive parallax
items.origin: The worked case is older than the term's exposition in the course: he points out that he had already given it in O Jardim das Aflições (1995) — Marx announcing a materialist philosophy and delivering one whose real substance is human action, with nature entering only as raw material. He generalises from it that a philosophy built on a parallax is not so much false as unrealisable, so its author ends up doing a third thing neither he nor his readers can name.
items.lineageNote: He takes the word from photography, where parallax is the divergence between the viewfinder and the lens — what you frame is not what the film records. The earliest located use is public rather than pedagogical, and applies the term to a class rather than to a thinker: at the Fórum da Liberdade in 2000 he diagnosed a country marking five hundred years of history by arguing about the present month's economic policy as a parallax, an abyss between life and consciousness. From there he draws the corollary he keeps: everyone in the debate reasons from the position of whoever decides, and reasoning from a position that is not really yours is what alienation means. The remedy he proposed was an autobiographical method — intellectuals asking not why Brazil went wrong but why they themselves did.

items.claim: His most widely deployed framework: four kinds of discourse — poetic, rhetorical, dialectical and analytical — graded by the certainty they can carry, which he treats as one scale rather than four separate disciplines. The order is a dependency, not a preference: he calls it the natural sequence of a human education, in which one learns to imagine and express the world before arguing about conduct, and argues about conduct before demonstrating anything. He read the Aristotelian corpus in that order and held that Aristotle's logic becomes unintelligible once it is amputated from his rhetoric.

items.claim: Empire is the recurring idea of Western history, and he traces its transmutations from the fall of Rome to the American expansion — each collapse followed by someone assembling the next one. His definition is the load-bearing part: an empire is a supranational organisation that does not federate nations but gathers forces from inside them, which is why it can operate against the interests of the very country that hosts it.
items.origin: Set out in O Jardim das Aflições (1995), of which he says a great part is a history of the transmutations of the idea of empire — a great part, not the whole: the book is subtitled an essay on materialism and civil religion, and the same pages carry the worked example of cognitive parallax. He calls it the one book whose literary structure he was able to compose deliberately, like a piece of music.
items.caveat: He notes that his account converges with Antonio Negri's Empire, written from the opposite political direction, and does not treat the convergence as embarrassing. He also says the book's narrative stops at the American empire and that everything after it needed the later work — see the three projects of global domination.
