items.title: The theory of Empire

items.claim: The sequel to the Empire thesis, and the framework he is best known for outside philosophy: the forces now contesting world power are not one conspiracy but three separate projects of global domination — which he names provisionally the Russo-Chinese, the Western, and the Islamic — of comparable weight, sometimes allied and sometimes at each other's throats. He insists nobody can say which will prevail, including the people running them.
items.origin: He presents it as the continuation of O Jardim das Aflições, whose narrative stops at the American empire: the 2011 debate with Aleksandr Dugin is, in his words, the book's proper complement, carrying the analysis forward to the present.
items.caveat: He rejects the 'masters of the universe' reading his own audience often draws from this — the point of a three-way contest is that no one is in control. He also insists 'Anglo-American' is the wrong name for the Western project.
items.revision: The naming shifts across the corpus. In 2009 he lists the communist project first and calls the third simply globalist; by 2013 the same three are 'the three globalisms'; and around 2020 he adds an observation rather than a correction, that the Western project is dismantling itself and the other two are collecting the winnings.

items.claim: In any act of knowing, three things are grasped at once and cannot be separated: the act itself, the thing known, and the conditions that make the act possible. His model is sight — you never see an object without also seeing the light, and the light that shows the object is the same light that reaches the eye. He argues this connection is what the whole edifice of logic rests on, since a certainty available only in words could never underwrite a proof.
items.origin: He dates the idea to an argument with the position that there is no reality outside human language, and calls it, in the same breath, one of his great discoveries and one of the worst written things he ever produced — a draft that circulated as a course handout and was never made into a book.
items.lineageNote: He built it to ground what he calls his radical intuitionism, and treats the near-universal symbolism of light and the sun as knowledge as evidence that the structure is not his invention but a description.

items.claim: Philosophy advances by landings rather than by schools: certain things, once seen, cannot be unseen, and reasoning below them is not disagreement but regression. Aristotle's distinction between form and matter is his standing example. The claim is normative, not historical — nobody has the right to argue beneath a landing. And a landing that is superseded is not thereby cancelled: climbing to a higher one, he says, in no way denies the value or the present importance of those below it, which he maintains even for a model whose founding premise he has just called plainly false.
items.caveat: Asked in class for the list of landings, he agreed it would be worth having and did not produce one. No general inventory exists — but for one field it does: in the opening session of the 2002 course he names the three models of the history of philosophy, rejects each, and then enumerates what each nonetheless makes it impermissible to ignore. That is the doctrine applied to a whole domain rather than asserted, and it is the only such application in the corpus.

items.title: The landings of philosophy

items.claim: History is only ever the history of agents that act, and most of the subjects historians write about cannot act. Brazil, he argues, has no history — it is the stage on which one happens, since a juridical-territorial unit has never done anything. The condition he says nobody had thought to state is continuity in time: an action exhausted inside one lifetime never enters history at all. What qualifies is a body that can train its successors to carry on a programme begun before they were born.
items.origin: He says he had to settle the question before he could ask whether historical knowledge explains anything at all about the divisions he was trying to describe, and calls the result an entirely new theory of history which he believes correct and irrefutable.
items.lineageNote: Dynasties are the case he develops furthest, and the one that carries the most weight in his political writing: aristocratic or plebeian families conscious of the durability of their own interests, who take children from the cradle and raise them to continue a programme — the Bourbons and the Tudors, and, on his reading, the Rockefellers and the Rothschilds. What makes a dynasty an agent is fidelity to dead mentors. He then treats the Bilderberg circle as a consortium of such dynasties rather than as an organisation, which is how this doctrine does the work his politics asks of it.
items.countNote: The list of kinds shifts between tellings. In 2009 he names the Catholic Church, Freemasonry, the Communist Party and dynastic families; in 2010 the great religions, initiatic societies, dynasties and the Communist Party; in 2011 he replaces the fourth with spiritual entities — God, angels and demons — and states there are no others. The four shown here are the human register, on which every telling agrees.
items.caveat: The fourth kind, in the fullest telling, is not human: he counts God, angels and demons as historical agents on the same criterion, since they too persist and act. Recorded as his claim. He also says himself that the theory has a problem — he never managed to apply it in a book that was entirely about history.

items.title: The collective imbecile
items.lineageNote: Two habits he singles out as the mechanism working. The first he calls by its old rhetorical name, argumentum ad ignorantiam, in the form Brazil gave it: what I have not heard of does not exist, said with an air of superiority — which he called, after a decade of newspaper polemic, the most frequently used argument he met. The second is an inversion of pedantry. Pedantry means parading knowledge you do not have; here, he says, having the knowledge is the pedantry, and asking an interlocutor to know the subject is treated as an attempt to humiliate him. What then stands in for the abandoned duties of intelligence is politeness: a cultivated debate comes to mean one in which everybody says foolish things courteously.

items.claim: An observation rather than a theory, and one his readers took up as a working category: the adolescent who believes he is rebelling is aiming at the weakest authority available — parents who love him and will do anything for him — while submitting completely to the strongest, the peers who will not. He puts the mechanism underneath it as a neurotic need for affection that produces group dependence, and says the political and moral language such a person uses is decoration over a much cruder motive.
structure: What it is: submission to the peer group
items.countNote: It is not an age. He is explicit that juvenile imbeciles are sixty and seventy years old: the essay describes a condition people carry into old age, not a phase they leave.
items.origin: A short article — he says he compressed the whole thing into a page and a half — published on his own site and later placed first in O Mínimo que Você Precisa Saber para Não Ser um Idiota (2013). He cites it in class the way one cites a reference, three times across four years, rather than re-explaining it.
items.lineageNote: He connects it to the American literature on peer pressure, which he says runs to thousands of books there and nothing at all in Brazil. It is also the illustration he reaches for when defining existential contradiction.
items.caveat: He never calls it a theory, and it is not one here. It earns its place as a described observation with an unusually clear trace of uptake: students bring it back to him unprompted across the whole run of the course — a parent asking how to keep small children from becoming juvenile imbeciles, a student connecting it to his exchange with the theologian Carlos Josaphat — using the phrase as a category rather than as a title.

items.claim: A contradiction not between two statements but inside a life: someone whose existence rests on an authority he is simultaneously trying to undermine — which, he argues, means the undermining is not fully serious, because the attack presupposes what it attacks. He sets it against merely logical contradiction, which he says any author will commit by inattention and which it is adolescent to go hunting for.

items.claim: His position in philosophy of law: that law is to be understood as guarantee — a limit protecting the person — rather than as a command issued by whoever holds power. He treats it as following from the four discourses, since what a legal text can establish depends on the kind of discourse it is.
structure: Law as a command from whoever holds power
Law as a guarantee — a limit protecting the person
items.origin: Set out in a course handout of his, 'O que é o direito', which he never developed into a book of his own.

He describes the thesis as departing from his handout and as his own position deepened by another hand.

items.title: Law as guarantee
The three constants of history
items.claim: Three tendencies, he says, hold across the whole of the human record and have never been falsified: population always grows; separated cultures move toward one another until they intercommunicate completely; and power integrates upward, the higher power destroying the intermediate powers with the help of the population below it. Globalisation is not a fourth thing added to these. It is what happens when people with the means to act understand the first three, at which point a process that was merely happening becomes deliberate and planned — so that, he says, globalisation is in a sense the name of human history itself.
items.origin: He credits each constant to someone else and claims only the assembly: the first to Malthus, the second to the geographer Ellsworth Huntington in The Mainsprings of Civilization, the third to Bertrand de Jouvenel in Du Pouvoir. He is emphatic that the Huntington in question is not Samuel Huntington of the clash of civilisations, whom he takes to be a descendant.
items.lineageNote: Jouvenel is the one he keeps returning to, and he treats Du Pouvoir as the standing answer to Benedetto Croce's history as the history of liberty: over the last four or five centuries state authority always comes out strengthened and the citizen below always weakened, and always on the pretext of democratising. Every levelling, on this reading, produces a worse hierarchy, because whoever distributes power is by that fact above everyone it is distributed to. The third constant is also where a second doctrine starts rather than ends: the growth of power is the premise from which he builds the difference of power as constitutive of the species, which is its own entry here. The credit for the growth of power belongs to this one.
items.caveat: He is elsewhere severe about exactly this kind of search. Civilisation, he says, is a figure of speech and not a scientific concept, so quantifying over civilisations is measurement applied to metaphor; and he states flatly that he believes no total interpretation of the historical process is possible. The constants are therefore offered as observed regularities of the human record, not as a law that explains it — a distinction he keeps, and one that the entry keeps with him.

expositions.where: Fórum da Liberdade, Porto Alegre — in the debate after his lecture
course lecture 22 — the fullest statement, with globalisation as a process made conscious and then voluntary

items.title: The three enemies of democracy
items.claim: He argues that democracy has only ever been definable against something, and that the something has changed three times: against the old regime, once the constitution of power became everyone's problem; against modern totalitarianism, which made the free circulation of knowledge a requirement Jefferson could not have imagined; and now against pseudo-democracy, since totalitarianism is finished as an idea and survives only under other names. Three things then threaten it, and all three arrive wearing its own vocabulary.
structure: Hegemony and the expanded state, sold as organised civil society
The extension of democracy past the political and juridical domain
items.origin: He names the third himself — 'what I call liberal economicism' — and describes it as an inverted version of Marxist economic determinism: the belief that liberalising the economy liberalises everything else automatically. His counter-example was China, which he said had been receiving a market economy for ten years while the government grew more repressive, and which the market economy was making rich enough to buy more weapons.
items.lineageNote: The first enemy is his reading of Gramsci: hegemony is the manufacture of a consensus so complete that nobody remembers it was ever argued, and the expanded state is the party-state under a new name, so that transferring public administration to organised civil society realises the totalitarian idea while sounding like its opposite. For the second he uses Georges Bernanos — democracy is not the opposite of dictatorship but its cause — and illustrates it with cultural democracy, which first distributes the highest values to everyone and then lets the beneficiaries decide the lowest are the highest.
items.caveat: He set out three and said he would leave the rest for another time, so the list is explicitly partial rather than closed. In the floor questions he added two more in passing: the medicalisation of society, and the idea that some international body should decide these matters — liberal doctrine, he said, was formed fighting the national state and finds itself defenceless against the world Leviathan now forming.

expositions.where: Fórum da Liberdade, Porto Alegre — 'Os desafios da democracia no século XXI'

items.title: Culture does not follow development
items.claim: Against the view that a country must first grow rich and then acquire a high culture, he holds that culture is the orientation of a life toward what is worth living for, and so is a condition of intelligence rather than one of its ornaments. Culture, on his etymology, means cultivation and cult together: something that improves, and something owed devotion. Both point past any state of affairs to what Plato called the supreme good. The Brazilian constitutional definition — whatever bears witness to a mode of existence — he places at the exact antipodes, because a mode of existence is a fact and not a value.
structure: First get rich, then acquire a culture
Culture is the sanity of intelligence, and comes first or not at all
items.origin: He raises it against Paulo Arantes's Um Departamento Francês de Ultramar, which asks why fifty years of the philosophy faculty at USP produced no philosopher and answers that a level of development must be reached first. Carvalho's reply is historical: no great burst of philosophical creativity has ever followed an economic boom. Athens produced the Academy amid socioeconomic decay and runaway inflation; scholasticism's largest contributions came from Ireland and England when England was five centuries from being a power; German idealism arrived when Germany was not yet a country.
items.lineageNote: He takes the supreme good from Plato and the psychological consequence from Viktor Frankl, whose camp observation — that those who came through were the ones with something to serve — he treats as evidence that the loss of a sense of existence lies under the neuroses. What replaces it he describes as a love of insignificance: Mário Ferreira dos Santos out of print while the theses accumulate on sambistas, and culture understood in three degraded senses at once — entertainment, commercial product, and party propaganda.
items.caveat: He is talking about Brazil and says so, and the argument is made from a platform funded by the industrialists whose Forum it was — the study of that Forum as an institution notes its corporate backing in exactly this period. The historical examples are offered as counter-cases to a claimed dependence, not as a demonstration that poverty produces philosophy, which he does not claim.

expositions.where: Fórum da Liberdade, Porto Alegre — the culture and development panel, debating Eduardo Bueno

items.title: The cycle of intervention
items.claim: He describes state intervention in labour relations as a closed loop that has been running in Brazil since Vargas, each turn creating the condition for the next. Government intervenes to protect employees; the charges decapitalise firms; the firms come to government for rescue; the rescue is paid for with higher taxes; higher taxes raise prices and cut purchasing power; the shortfall requires new social programmes; the programmes require more tax. His point is not that any single step is wrong but that seventy years of it should have been enough to draw the conclusion, and that failing to draw a conclusion from your own experience is a defect of sight rather than of information.
structure: The state intervenes to protect employees
Taxes rise to pay for the rescue
items.origin: Stated at the Fórum da Liberdade in 2005, on a panel about the culture of work, against Oded Grajew — a founder of the World Social Forum, the Porto Alegre meetings this Forum was created to answer. Grajew had left before his turn, which Carvalho remarked on.
items.lineageNote: He then argued that the debate itself was staged wrongly: the Brazilian argument imitates Conservatives against Labour inside a settled constitutional order, when the real question is which forces confront each other. On the liberal side he counted the industrialist Jorge Gerdau and a handful of Rio Grande do Sul businessmen; on the other, the FARC, the Chilean MIR, the Foro de São Paulo with what he put at eighty-four member organisations, the European Union, the United Nations and the Ford, Rockefeller and MacArthur foundations. It is the argument his later work on global projects is built from, five years before he made it abroad.
items.caveat: The second half is a set of factual claims, several of which are checkable and one of which does not survive checking. He said a declaration signed by Lula in 2002, shortly before he became a candidate, absolved the FARC and accused the Colombian government of state terrorism. The FARC is named in none of the nineteen held final declarations of the Foro de São Paulo, and the 2002 declaration is dated after Lula had already won the election. The cycle above is his structural argument and stands or falls separately from that.

expositions.where: Fórum da Liberdade, Porto Alegre — 'A cultura do trabalho', with Suri Ratnapala and Oded Grajew

items.title: Philosophy as a project
items.claim: Philosophy was not born finished — and he argues that everything else follows from saying so. What is not born finished cannot have appeared as a completed structure, only as a project or an ambition to be realised; and its founders must have known it was one, or philosophical discussion could never have taken the form it does, validating and invalidating doctrines piecemeal where a religion would call the same move heresy. From which he draws a single conclusion about method: there is only one scientifically valid way to tell the history of philosophy, as the succession of stages in realising an original project — and of the attempts to alter, impugn or replace it. He presents the three principles as apodictic rather than empirical, established before opening any history of philosophy rather than inferred from one.
structure: Therefore it appeared as a project
Its founders knew it was one
Heirs are not bound to keep it intact
Even faithful heirs may be forced off course
items.caveat: He claims the method satisfies the Hegelian demand for unity of movement without Hegel's error of imposing unity on events that have none — because where the facts yield only the unity of a problem, of a confusion or of an enigma, that is what gets recorded. Whether it escapes the objection is not something this project adjudicates.

expositions.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 1 — the three principles, the consequence for method, and the three conditions of any human project

items.title: Against 'a man of his time'
items.claim: Calling someone a man of his time he judges a very great piece of nonsense — and says the person who says it believes he is doing history while doing the exact opposite of history. Nobody can be exclusively of his own time; if everyone were, there would be no history at all. His case is Brentano, a nineteenth-century philosopher whose own century must be inferred from indirect signs while Aristotle is everywhere in him: an influence two thousand years old outweighing a contemporary one. What makes history possible is instead a capacity he calls the sense of eternity — being able to put one's head outside one's own time and judge it whole, the same faculty by which a person judges his own life and says he took a wrong turn. Without it we are a drop of water in a river, unable to see where it is going.
structure: No one is only of his own time
But you must know where and when you live
items.caveat: Two things keep this from being a simple rejection of historical situatedness, and both are his. He notes that the phrase is never used of Stalin or Hitler, because calling them men of their time would mean conceding that we produced them, and nobody wants that responsibility. And he demands the opposite of indifference to one's own moment: your whole intellectual and personal life, he says, has to unfold inside an alert consciousness of the real situation you are living in — you have to know where and when you are living. What he rejects is not situatedness but its counterfeit, being the man of the day, the week or the month with a view of the world bounded by whatever is being talked about.

expositions.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 1 — including the request that his future biographers never write it of him, and the reductio that if only history exists then history does not
course lecture 31 — you do not need to be a man of your time, but you do need to know where and when you are living

In an undated later lecture he calls it his final message in the documentary made about him, and says O Jardim das Aflições illustrates it structurally. items.title: Intellectual teratology
items.claim: His own coinage, and he introduces it as one: the study of failed alterations to the philosophical project — failed not through accident or incompetence, but because the statement of the alteration already announced something impossible to do, and whoever made it did not notice. His worked example is the historicism he has just dissected: a doctrine that saws through the branch it is sitting on, or cuts off its own feet to walk better.

expositions.where: Curso História Essencial da Filosofia, session 1 — the term introduced, with self-refuting historicism as the case

items.title: The difference of power
items.originalTerm: A fenomenologia do poder / a diferença de poder
items.claim: That the immeasurable difference of power between members of the species is not a political arrangement but a constitutive element of the species itself. He reaches it by joining two authors: Jouvenel's finding in Du Pouvoir that power always grows, and Ibn Khaldun on prophetic authority, which he says three times is what put him on the line of enquiry. He then reports going to look for the same thing in animals, and concludes from the contrast that the maximum of violence one human being does to another is always statal — no criminal, gang or murderer kills as many as a government — so that the juridical ordering of society tracks the increase in killing, modern democracies included.
structure: The difference of power is constitutive of the species
The maximum of violence is always statal
items.origin: He tells it as a moment of discovery, and calls it o estalo — the click. Reading Jouvenel on the growth of power alongside Ibn Khaldun on prophetic authority, the two struck together and gave him the constitutive claim. He arrives at the same conclusion by a second and independent route elsewhere, through Raskolnikov rather than through Jouvenel, and there names it as his own: one of the themes of his political philosophy, the theme of the difference of power.
items.caveat: Two things this entry records as his and does not adjudicate. The first is a factual claim about animals: that zoologists know of only some twelve hundred species in which a member kills another of the same species, that gorillas settle by display and wolves by the position of the tail, and that homo homini lupus therefore libels the wolf. The second is a qualification he attaches to the conclusion and which is easy to drop: the difference between democracy and dictatorship on this measure he calls very relative and quantitative — real, but not deep enough to mark a difference of essence.

expositions.where: course lecture 70 — the discovery narrative end to end: Jouvenel, Ibn Khaldun, the click, the zoology, and the statal conclusion
course lecture 111 — the difference of power as a structural and permanent component of human life
course lecture 79 — the most systematic statement: power as capacity for action, and two arguments that the difference is unabolishable
course lecture 115 — names it as one of the themes of his own political philosophy, reached through Raskolnikov

items.countNote: Lectures 79 and 115 both carry unresolved date disagreements in the corpus — 79's header reads 2012 against an index, filenames and a surrounding sequence that all support 2010 — so both are entered unverified. The chain runs end to end only in lecture 70; the zoology, the licence to kill and the statal conclusion appear in no other file.

works.note: The books in order of first publication. He wrote for a living from before he was eighteen and published for forty years, and the shape of that output is an argument in itself: a decade of astrology and symbolism, a burst of small press books from the institute he ran, the polemics that made him a public name, a course sold as thirty-two volumes, and finally a newspaper column collected into ten volumes while he was already teaching from Virginia. Re-editions are shown only where the book changed publisher, title or shape; otherwise the first edition stands for the work.

Where it disagrees with other sources the entry says so rather than choosing silently. Everything after 2018 is past the CV's own horizon and rests on the publisher's catalogue and secondary lists, so it is marked as the weaker tier it is. Article-level work is not listed: he published in the press for decades and no reliable index of it exists, so the columns are given as runs rather than as a list of pieces that would be arbitrary.

items.title: O Crime da Madre Agnes, ou: A Confusão entre Espiritualidade e Psiquismo
O Profeta da Paz: Estudos sobre a Interpretação Simbólica da Vida do Profeta Mohammed
items.note: It won a prize and was never published, and he explains why. On air in 2007 he says the competition rules promised to publish the winner; the jury told him that because his book was not an Islamic book they could not publish it, and gave him the cash equivalent instead — money he used for a trip he had been wanting to take. He dates the episode himself to '86, 87' and names the awarding body as Al-Azhar, in Saudi Arabia. Two years later he tells it again more briefly, with the jury's words as: not an orthodox Islamic book, we cannot approve all of its content, but it is the one that won. Elsewhere he describes the work as a symbolic exegesis of some ahadith of the Prophet, and as a study of the origins of Islam. Later still he disowns it — one of his two earliest studies, no longer representative of his thought, needing much revision because he had leaned on Idries Shah, whom he came to judge a complete charlatan. So the absence of a publisher is not a gap in the record: by his account there was never an edition to find.
items.sourceNote: His CV for the title and the prize; True Outspeak #49 (2007) for the rules, the refusal and the payment; True Outspeak #146 (2009) for the jury's wording; course lectures 105 and 165, both reviewed, for the recognition; a later unreviewed lecture for the disavowal.
